syllabus: The ever-increasing volume of media data such as videos, audio, and text has accelerated the onset of the Big Data era. One of the key reasons behind the success of data-driven machine learning methods, especially deep learning, in fields like computer vision and natural language processing is the extraction of intelligent information from Big Data. With the advent of Big Data, our thought process has shifted from the former knowledge-driven model to a data-driven paradigm. Moreover, the interaction, influence, and integration among multimodal, multidimensional, and heterogeneous data sources have endowed Big Data with more valuable information. The rapid development of artificial intelligence poses many challenges for current Big Data intelligence analysis, driving us toward a dual-driven mode of thinking that combines both data-driven and knowledge-driven approaches. Big Data Intelligence forms the foundation of today?s Big Data and AI, where discovering reliable knowledge from uncertain and complex data to guide intelligent decision-making has become an essential capability for researchers and managers alike. Consequently, it is highly important for graduate students to grasp these concepts, knowledge, and skills. This course aims to help students understand and master the theories and methods related to data science and artificial intelligence. Specifically, it seeks to enhance students? knowledge and abilities in the following three areas: 1. Mastering the theories and methods of data science. 2. Mastering the theories and methods related to artificial intelligence. 3. Integrating data science and AI theories to apply existing (or improved) algorithms for efficient Big Data processing and analysis. The course content covers fundamental data analysis and processing methods in data science (including regression analysis, probability theory, and other statistical machine learning theories) as well as predicate logic, deep learning, reinforcement learning, meta-learning, automated machine learning, and other AI theories and methods. Classroom lectures and additional assessments will be used to achieve the instructional objectives.

syllabus: M & As are an important strategic behavior for the rapid development and value promotion of modern firms. How to realize firm value 1 + 1 > 2 and 1-1 > 0 through corporate M & A and restructuring activities? The course will comprehensively introduce the motivation of M & As, the practical operation process of M & A deals, and how to make scientific and optimal decisions of an M & A transaction. The course will include 8 modules: M & A motivation, due diligence, M & A transaction structure design, M & A valuation, corporate control right design and competition, post transaction integration, other firm restructuring methods, and the new trend of M & A transactions and industrial development under the transformation of the digital economy. The course builds a complete knowledge system of M & A through 8 modules. The course not only includes the basic theoretical knowledge related to M & As, but also will lead you to understand how Geely Automobile, a Chinese private enterprise, evaded capital market risks and successfully acquired Daimler, the parent company of Mercedes Benz automobile, a major international company; how did a Chinese firm acquire the world's largest listed company of Kerr health products in Canada; how did Cisco, an internationally renowned high-tech company, maintain 30 years of global technology leadership through collaborative M & A with Sequoia Capital's "listed company + PE" for many years. Finally, the course will help you understand from theory to practice how firms can enhance and create value through M&A and corporate restructuring, and become an expert of capital markets.

syllabus: Firms compete in Consumer & Business Markets to sell their products & services, and they also compete in Capital Markets for the resources required to operate their business. Investors provide the capital (resources) to companies with the expectation that they will earn a competitive return on their capital and compensate themfor risk. A consumer or business manager is continuously faced with financial choices and meeting the demands of both of these arenas of competition. For the consumer these choices include, among others, financing a purchase, saving for retirement and evaluating investment products. For a business manager the choices include deciding which projects to pursue and alternative approaches to provide funds for these projects. Finance is the study of a framework that can be used to evaluate these choices consistent with the necessity of competing for investor capital. Regardless of your ultimate career, a solid understanding of the fundamentals of finance, will serve you well.

syllabus: Sustainable development (SD) refers to a holistic approach to economic, social, and environmental progress that aims to meet the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future gen- erations to meet their own needs. It encompasses the idea of balancing economic growth, social equity, and environmental protection to ensure that development occurs in a way that is viable in the long term. It aims to improve quality of life across economic, social, and environmental realms without compromising the earth?s fragile ecosystems. This balanced approach is critical for human-ity? long-term prosperity and survival. Implementing sustainable practices now helps ensure the viability of the planet for generations to come. This course highlights the conflicts associated with the concept of SD on the national and the glob-al scales. The practical solutions to sustainable development will be examined in different national contexts and at the global level. The topical issues, such as climate change, energy transition and food & neutrition, are selected for in-depth discussion as these issues render profound impact on the sustainability of our planet, thus the survival of future generations.

There may be over 10^22 stars in the universe and modern estimates indicate that most of these stars are (or were) accompanied by planets. The aim of this course is to understand the fundamental properties of stars and planets from elementary physical principles. This course is organized according to several modules: 1. Introduction to key Astronomy concepts 2. Matter under astrophysical conditions 3. Planet and stellar Birth 4. Planet and stellar Evolution and Death 5. Planet and stellar Atmospheres 6. Planet and stellar Dynamics Student participation and problem sets play an instrumental part throughout the course. The classical instruction will be further supplemented by presentations and a report from students on a topic of their choosing related to the field of stars and planets.

syllabus: This is a course of Chinese Civilization in which the basic requirements include both teaching within lesson and watching museums without lesson. In this course some dynasties or topics (Confucianism, Buddhism, Taoism and Sino west Cultural Exchanges) are selected as the teaching subjects , and these dynasties and topics are represents of Chinese civilization. Students are encouraged to get the interrelated understanding and sensitive perception of Chinese civilization. The teaching ideas of this course are as follows : (1) Formation and development of Chinese Civilization are the outcome of dynamic interactions between. pre agricultural civilization, agricultural civilization, nomadic civilization, maritime civilization and industrial civilization. The capacities of material production and social organization are two basic foundations; (2) the material quality and its processing technology are the key for the understanding Chinese civilization and they provide material foundation of Chinese cosmology and view of nature . The development from jade to the bronze, and then to iron and porcelain, are the embodiment of Chinese spirit and its technique. When we are watching museum, what we get are not only appreciation of the beauty of material quality and art design, but also the apprehension of Chinese social values. This is a slow cultural evolution which could only be measured with the scale of millennium . 3 Chinese civilization has a peculiar wisdom of social organization. These wisdom are embodied in the scholarships as Confucianism, Taoism and Legalism. With the help of classical learning and the family state spirit , Chinese civilization established a large cultural system which are characteristic of meritocracy,hardworking and frugality. (4) Chinese civilization are divided into three periods: (a) from the beginning to the end of East Han Dynaty; (b) from Weijin dynasties to the end of Qing dynasty; (c) From 1911 to today. The contents of this course are as follows: (1) pre agricutural civilization; 2 agricultural 3 competitions between agricultural and nomadic civilization ; (4) Rise of maritime civilization and its dilemma; 5 Rise of the Chinese industrial civilization;

syllabus: Why do people hold money? What determines the amount of money people hold relatively to other assets? What role do banks and other financial institutions play in the economy? Why isn't there just one world currency? How does the monetary policy work in an economy? These are the fundamental questions in monetary economics, and the purpose of the course is to provide students with the comprehensive analysis of the money markets and modern monetary policy. Throughout the course, a special emphasis will be put on using simple mathematical models to answer the questions we are interested in, rather than focusing on institutional details, which traditionally are the focus of money and banking courses. This course is designed as a survey of the basic theories in monetary economics for advanced undergraduate students. A good skill in mathematics will be helpful for the understanding of the lectures. Among the topics to be covered include: money demand and money supply, inflation and optimal quantity of money, international monetary system, Banking, monetary policy transmission mechanism, strategy of monetary policy and optimal monetary policy, time inconsistency problem in monetary policy. For each topic covered, a core body of theories, issues, and evidence will be presented and discussed.

syllabus: This course explores environmental issues such as intellectual history, global history, and microhistory from a broad historical perspective and different methodological frameworks. Students will become familiar with current historical issues related to the environment (including the "Anthropocene") and become familiar with different approaches to delving into historical issues. Topics discussed in this course include: What is the relationship between history and the environment? Does the environment shape people, or do humans shape the environment? To what extent has technology changed the environment? What is the relationship between the environment and food production? How has industrialization changed our conception of the environment and food? Agricultural topics are then the proper meaning of this course. For example, from the beginning of time immemorial, farmers cultivated the land. But the peasant itself is conceptualized and seen as a recent process on a historical epistemological problem. In addition, peasants were assigned to the periphery, while the central areas were considered the poles of civilization. Can we accept this conceptual framework? If food production is on the margins, how can it play a central role in our daily lives?

syllabus: Part One: Normal-form games Part Two: Extensive games Part Three: Bayesian games Part Four: Mechanism design Course Description: This course will serve as an introduction to game theory: a vastly popular branch of microeconomic theory concentrating on interactions of players. Concretely, it can be divided into two phases. On the first phase, we will focus on the "modeling and analysis" of games. We will show how to turn an economic situation into game theoretical models and analyze its solution, i.e., how to play the game. The corresponding topics are: normal-form games, extensive-form games, repeated games and games with incomplete information. On the second phase, we will focus on the "design" of games. We will provide various frameworks to design a game in certain realistic environments and use techniques learnt from the previous phase to analyze design performance. The increasing number of media data such as video, audio, and text has accelerated the era of big data. Mining intelligent information from big data is one of the essential reasons for the success of current data-driven machine learning methods represented by deep learning in computer vision, natural language processing and other fields. The arrival of big data has changed our way of thinking from the past knowledge-driven to today's data-driven, and the interaction, influence and penetration between multi-modal, multi-dimensional, multi-source heterogeneous data are giving big data more valuable information; The rapid development of artificial intelligence has brought many challenges to the current big data intelligent analysis, and is prompting us to change to a dual-drive way of thinking that combines data-driven and knowledge-driven. Big data intelligence is the foundation of our big data and artificial intelligence today, and finding reliable knowledge from uncertain complex data to guide our intelligent decision- making has now become an essential capability for scientific and technological research and managers. Therefore, it is of great importance for graduate students to master these concepts, knowledge and abilities. This course will strive to enable students to understand and master the relevant theories and methods of data science and artificial intelligence, and will strive to improve students' knowledge and ability in the following three aspects: 1. Be able to combine data science and artificial intelligence related theories, and use known (or improved) algorithms to efficiently process and analyze big data. The cutting-edge research about deep learning will also be discussed. Specifically, we will study the typical models including the multi-layer Perceptron, convolutional neural network, self-organizing map, Elman recurrent neural network, long short-term memory network, Hopfield network, restricted Boltzmann network, deep belief network, variational auto- encoder, generative adversarial network, etc. Interesting applications of these models will be discussed. Python, a simple programming language and Pytorch, a neural network software, will be briefly introduced. In the end of the course, you are required to design a deep learning model for solving a practical problem, which can be chosen from a set of problems provided by the teacher or proposed by yourself, submit a course project report, and present the results in a poster. English is the teaching language.
textbooks: Deep Learning by Ian Goodfellow and Yoshua Bengio and Aaron Courville, 2016

syllabus: Deep learning is an important part of the artificial intelligence discipline and one of the main driving forces behind the resurgence of artificial intelligence in recent years. This course will introduce the concept and history of deep learning, explain its basic principles and typical models in depth, and discuss its research frontiers. The specific content includes models such as multi-layer perceptron, convolutional neural network, Elman feedback neural network, long short-term memory network, deep belief network, and generative confrontation network, as well as their applications in the fields of computer vision, speech processing, and natural language processing. The course will also briefly introduce the basics of python programming and the use of neural network tool software Pytorch/Mindspore. At the end of the semester, students need to build their own model to solve a practical application problem (optional), write and submit a course report, and present it through posters or slides Schedule: 1 Basic concepts and history of deep learning 2 Mathematics, machine learning, and Python basics 3 Regression and classification 4 Multilayer Perceptron and Training Techniques I 5 Convolutional Neural Network-I 6 Convolutional Neural Network-II 7 Training Tips II and Getting Started with Pytorch/Mindspore 8 Application of deep learning in computer vision 9 Feedback Neural Network 10 word embeddings 11 sentence processing 12 Deep Belief Network 13 Generative Adversarial Networks 14 cutting-edge topics 15 course assignment report

syllabus: This course will explore the encoding and decoding processing, adaptation and learning, communication and computation of information from multiple levels such as individual neurons, neural networks, and neural systems, in order to understand the cognitive function of the brain by establishing computational models. The main content includes: (1) Fundamentals of Neuroscience: Introduction to some basic concepts of neuroscience. (2) Encoding and decoding: single cell release rate encoding, single cell time encoding, population encoding, inverse correlation methods, and simple cell receptive field mathematical models; Analysis of human-machine interface, EEG, and fMRI data. (3) Bayesian inference in the brain: The theory and methods of Bayesian inference, continuous variable inference, and discrete variable inference. (4) Neuron models: electrical properties of neurons, Hodgkin Huxley model, Integrate and Fire model. (5) Neural networks: feedforward networks, recursive networks, excitation suppression networks; Hopfield network, Boltzmann machine, restricted Boltzmann machine. (6) Plasticity and learning: Hebb rule, covariance rule, BCM rule, synaptic regularization, discharge time dependent plasticity (STDP), self-organizing imprinting learning, perceptual machine learning, and constrained Boltzmann machine learning. (7) Natural image statistics: The statistical characteristics of natural images, principal component analysis, and the formation of central peripheral receptive fields; Independent component analysis and the formation of simple cell receptive fields. (6) Deep learning: Briefly introduce multi-layer perceptrons, deep belief networks, convolutional neural networks, and their applications in image classification and speech recognition. Emphasis will be placed on the interaction between deep learning and neuroscience. syllabus: Since humans learned to make tools, they have been trying to build more and more powerful automatic machines to help people complete various tasks. This process has promoted the development of a series of important disciplines (from mechanics, mechanics, to computer science) and industries (from agriculture, industry, to information industry). Today's world is in a new round of intelligent wave and industrial revolution, and emerging disciplines (artificial intelligence, machine learning, etc.) and industries (autonomous driving, intelligent robots, etc.) are booming. Automatic machines that integrate current intelligent technology can be called intelligent systems, and robots (including unmanned vehicles, robotic arms, legged robots, etc.) are their important physical carriers. This course will systematically explain how to design the "brain" of intelligent systems and robots from the perspectives of artificial intelligence, machine learning, robotics, and control, including how to model the environment and system, plan and control, and how to learn adaptively. The course content covers topics such as dynamic system modeling, optimal control, trajectory planning, reinforcement learning, estimation and perception. Through the study of this course, students can not only systematically master the main theories in the field of robotics, have a deep understanding of the role and function of artificial intelligence in it, but also practice and apply theoretical knowledge through simulation or physical robot experimental training. Schedule: 1. Course introduction 2. Rigid body motion 3. Robot kinematics 4. Robot planning (HW1 part 1) 5. Robot dynamics 6. Robot control (HW1 part 2) 7. Model predictive control and optimization basics 8. Optimal control 9. Mid-term exam 10. Trajectory optimization (HW2) 11. Reinforcement learning 12. Deep reinforcement learning (HW3) 13. State estimation 14. Advanced topics 15. Course project presentation

syllabus: Course Description: Modern cryptography aims to protect information privacy, integrity and authentication. In this course, we first review basis of discrete probability, algebra and classical cryptography. Then there are three sections remaining: (1) symmetric key encryption (e.g., block cipher), (2) public key encryption, (3) cryptographic protocols (e.g., key exchange, digital signature) and applications (e.g., blockchain). Except for the cryptographic mechanisms, we would also introduce the related cryptanalytic methods and implementations. This course has course projects in group of two or three students, mainly about applications of cryptography or side channel attack to cryptographic system.

syllabus: AIOps stands for Autonomous IT Operations or Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations. It is a interdisciplinary research field between Machine Learning and Systems/Networking, which is why this course had this historical title ?Advanced Network Management?. Imagine that you are running a large Internet-based service with hundreds of thousands of servers and many software modules. You want to achieve 99.999% service reliability, but the terabytes of machine-generated monitoring data and hundreds of operators (IT operation engineers) alone won?t get you there, because of the high complexity and sheer scale of the software/hardware system and the vast amount of machine-generated data. What do we do? Machine Learning to the rescue! This course will cover the latest progress in major topics of AIOps using case studies from recent research papers in top conferences in all major computer science fields, including Machine Learning, Data Mining, System/Networking, Software Engineering, Database, Multimedia, etc. Through these case studies, we will show how the latest Machine Learning Algorithms are applied to solve the unique challenges in AIOps. The basics of these Machine Learning algorithms will be briefly reviewed in an easy-to-understand way, without going through the detailed theory behind them. Thus by the end of the course, you will be able to learn roughly how these algorithms work, and how it can be applied to solve real-world problems. 1. Deep Learning 2. Deep Neural Networks for Time Series or Sequence 3. Deep Generative Model (VAE, GAN) 4. Deep Reinforcement Learning 5. Natural Language Processing 6. Causal Inference The major topics of AIOps are the following: 1. Anomaly Detection in Time Series, Logs (semi-structured text), Traces (program execution trace), and Graphs 2. Anomaly Localization 3. Failure/Event Prediction 4. Causal Inference and its application in Root Cause Analysis. 5. Resource Allocation

syllabus: The increasing number of media data such as video, audio, and text has accelerated the era of big data. Mining intelligent information from big data is one of the essential reasons for the success of current data-driven machine learning methods represented by deep learning in computer vision, natural language processing and other fields. The arrival of big data has changed our way of thinking from the past knowledge-driven to today's data-driven, and the interaction, influence and penetration between multi-modal, multi-dimensional, multi-source heterogeneous data are giving big data more valuable information; The rapid development of artificial intelligence has brought many challenges to the current big data intelligent analysis, and is prompting us to change to a dual-drive way of thinking that combines data-driven and knowledge-driven. Big data intelligence is the foundation of our big data and artificial intelligence today, and finding reliable knowledge from uncertain complex data to guide our intelligent decision-making has now become an essential capability for scientific and technological research and managers. Therefore, it is of great importance for graduate students to master these concepts, knowledge and abilities. This course will strive to enable students to understand and master the relevant theories and methods of data science and artificial intelligence, and will strive to improve students' knowledge and ability in the following three aspects: 1. Master the theories and methods of data science. 2. Master the theoretical methods related to artificial intelligence. 3. Be able to combine data science and artificial intelligence related theories, and use known (or improved) algorithms to efficiently process and analyze big data. The scope of knowledge of this course covers basic methods of data analysis and processing in data science, statistical machine learning theories such as regression analysis and probability theory, and artificial intelligence theories and methods such as predicate logic, deep learning, reinforcement learning, meta-learning, and automatic machine learning. This course will achieve the teaching purpose through classroom lectures and other assessment methods. The development of the Internet makes more and more students get interested in related technologies. The Internet is facing regeneration, and the key technologies of new generation Internet are in dire need of spread. The course aims to enable students further understand and master the key technologies (including technical principles and specific realization) of new generation Internet after an overall understanding, and tentatively cultivate students? research ability in this field.

syllabus: This course adopts a lean operations perspective to examine how production systems can achieve sustainable competitive advantage. It begins with production strategy and capacity planning, incorporating the impact of learning curves to support efficient resource utilisation. Demand forecasting is then addressed through both qualitative and quantitative methods to enable more responsive and waste-minimising planning. Integrated planning and master production scheduling are explored as tools for aligning production capacity with fluctuating demand while maintaining flow and reducing excess inventory. Inventory control theory focuses on determining order quantities, reorder points, and order cycles under both deterministic and uncertain demand, including the use of batch discount strategies and ABC classification to prioritise materials management. Material requirements planning is examined through decomposition algorithms and production batch sizing techniques that support coordinated, pull-oriented production. Operations scheduling introduces key scheduling objectives and rules, presenting standard algorithms for both flow shop and make-to-order environments to enhance throughput and delivery performance. Lean production principles are emphasised through the study of kanban systems, level production, quick changeovers, autonomous quality control, flexible manufacturing, and continuous improvement. Finally, constraint management is addressed through synchronised production planning that focuses on system bottlenecks to improve overall flow and operational efficiency.

syllabus: International Business is the basic introductory course to international business and management. Its goal is to familiarize students with key aspects of the international political, economic, and institutional environment in which firms operate. The course is intended for students who are interested in managing, advising or analyzing global operations for both mature companies and startups. This course is designed to familiarize students with the essential concepts and practices of international business. Through a combination of lectures, case studies, and interactive discussions and final exam, students will explore how various factors influence business strategy, operations, and performance on a global scale. The course begins with an overview of the global landscape at a macro level, covering different aspects of international trade and trade policy. We then turn to foreign investment and the factors that influence the foreign investment decisions of multinational firm managers. syllabus: Firms compete in Consumer & Business Markets to sell their products & services, and they also compete in Capital Markets for the resources required to operate their business. Investors provide the capital (resources) to companies with the expectation that they will earn a competitive return on their capital and compensate themfor risk. A consumer or business manager is continuously faced with financial choices and meeting the demands of both of these arenas of competition. For the consumer these choices include, among others, financing a purchase, saving for retirement and evaluating investment products. For a business manager the choices include deciding which projects to pursue and alternative approaches to provide funds for these projects. Finance is the study of a framework that can be used to evaluate these choices consistent with the necessity of competing for investor capital. Regardless of your ultimate career, a solid understanding of the fundamentals of finance, will serve you well.

syllabus: Empirical Finance is a course for senior undergraduate students who are interested in applying real data to test classical asset pricing theories and in the applications of econometric methods to financial problems. This course mainly contains two parts: ?empirical asset pricing? and ?applied econometrics?. The first part discusses how to apply real data or simulation methods to test classical financial theories, including equity valuation, portfolio management analysis, CAPM model, Fama-Macbeth regression, Fama-French-Carhart factor model, Arbitrage Pricing Theory, and multi-factor pricing models for fixed income securities. The second part helps students review basic econometric theory, and further talks about more advanced time-series and panel data models, including ARIMA model, GARCH model, fixed/random effect models, and varying-coefficient models. syllabus: This course offers an in-depth exploration of the principles, architectures, and optimization techniques that underpin modern AI systems. As Transformer architectures and Large Language Models (LLMs) become foundational in industry and research, the scalability, performance, and efficiency of ML systems have emerged as key enablers for innovation. The course emphasizes the co-design of algorithms, compilers, and hardware to achieve efficient training and inference across heterogeneous computing platforms. Core topics include the computational characteristics of deep learning workloads, GPU and CPU architectural differences, memory hierarchy and hardware-aware optimization methods such as fusion, parallelization, caching, blocking, and pipelining. Students will further study graph- level compilation, attention-level acceleration (e.g., FlashAttention, sparsity, low-rank approximation), and neural-level optimizations including pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation. In addition, the course introduces distributed training strategies such as data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism, as well as recent frameworks like ZeRO, FSDP, and Alpa for large-scale deployment. Advanced topics on post-training enhancement, including reinforcement learning?based fine-tuning, reward modeling, and parameter- efficient adaptation, will also be discussed. Through proposal development, paper reproduction, and system implementation projects, students will gain hands-on experience in analyzing performance bottlenecks, designing scalable training and inference pipelines, and building end-to-end machine learning systems that integrate algorithmic innovation with hardware efficiency.

Through this course, students will understand the key problems, state-of-the-art solutions as well as limitations in the current 3D visual computing area. syllabus: Signals and systems, the characteristics of signals, the properties of systems, the responses of systems to input signals, etc., are common problems encountered in various academic fields. This course focuses on learning the basic concepts, theories, and methods for analyzing the characteristics of signals and the properties of systems. With the widespread application of computers and digital systems, a large number of problems related to the analysis of discrete signals and discrete systems have emerged. Based on the basic analysis methods for continuous signals and continuous systems, this course further studies the basic analysis methods for discrete signals and discrete systems, with system analysis limited to linear time-invariant systems. The methods of signal and system analysis covered in this course include time domain, frequency domain, and complex frequency domain. Time domain analysis: convolution for continuous systems and discrete systems, solving differential equations for continuous systems and difference equations for discrete systems. Frequency domain analysis: Fourier series and Fourier transforms for continuous and discrete signals, system frequency response characteristics, discrete Fourier transform (DFT) and fast Fourier transform (FFT) for computer applications. Complex frequency domain analysis: Laplace transform for continuous signals and continuous system analysis based on the Laplace transform, Z transform for discrete signals and discrete system analysis based on the Z transform, system function. This course emphasizes the relationships between different types of signal transformations.

syllabus: Data mining automatically and intelligently extracts the knowledge and information hidden in massive amounts of data. It is an inevitable outcome of big data processing and has become an indispensable technique for data processing and solving real-world problems. The development of artificial intelligence, especially large-model technologies, has further advanced data mining techniques. From smartphones to modern CPUs and GPUs, and even the world?s largest supercomputers, parallel computing is everywhere. Course topics include: An overview of parallel computing, serial program optimization, parallel programming models and principles, multithreaded programming and optimization, multiprocess programming and optimization, GPU programming and optimization, as well as performance analysis and modeling of parallel programs.

syllabus: Game theory is the foundation of almost all modern economic theory. It is one of the most interesting courses in undergraduate economics. Emerged originally as a field of mathematics, it has been successfully applied to all fields of economics. Furthermore, game theory also plays an increasing role in other social sciences such as philosophy, law and politics, and in natural science such as evolutionary biology and computer science, etc. This course is an introduction to game theory, which puts emphasis in introducing basic game-theoretic analysis, including the conception, analytic techniques and applications for each type of games. We will discuss static games with perfect information, static games with imperfect information, and dynamic games with or without perfect information. Most class sessions will be delivered in English and will consist of both ?hands- on? experiences in structured strategic situations as well as lectures about the theory underlying these situations. syllabus: Among branches of modern logic, modal logic provides a nice balance of expressivity and complexity, allowing it to be applied widely and extensively in many fields ranging from humanities to software design. In this course, ideas and methods of modal logic will be introduced along with its famous applications in modeling time, knowledge, necessity, and social behaviors. In this thread, student will be led into environments similar to research, in which ideas and needs from theoretical side and practical side frequently interact. Pointers will be given to standard textbooks/handbooks as well as notable papers, and with knowledge and skills introduced in this course, students with further interests should in principle be able to explore by their own. This course aims to student who more or less have learnt some logic, but this is not strictly required. No mandatory prerequisites required. Students are expected to have a certain understanding of the language and semantics of propositional and predicate logic, be able to correctly use mathematical concepts such as sets, graphs, relations, and functions, and be interested in philosophical issues and willing to participate in discussions.

syllabus: The goal of this course is to build the connection between the fundamental physics and computing algorithms through digital circuits and processors. This course covers the basic concepts of electronic engineering from digital logic circuits to microcomputer processors in a systematic and simplified manner. The class is divided into two sections. The first section of digital circuits describes how digital circuits work at the gate and flip-flop levels and contains the analysis and design of combinational and sequential circuits. The second section describes micro-processor organization and architecture. It introduces the fundamental concepts such as computer instruction sets, ALU, controller, registers and I/O. A single- cycle processor and another pipelined version will be discussed. The textbooks, slides, lectures, homework assignments and exams will be in English.

syllabus: Software project management is the art and science of planning and leading software projects. It is a sub-discipline of project management in which software projects are planned, monitored and controlled. Using software development life cycle and process groups as two main threads, this course introduces the procedures and methods of software project management, which will help keep projects under control, and produce software with required functions in shorter time, higher quality and predicable cost. This course follows the ten Project Management Knowledge Areas that are defined in PMBOK - integration, scope, schedule, cost, quality, resource, communications, risk, procurement, and stakeholder - using the experiences of real-life businesses involving software. The students are organized in groups to do the homework and give presentations. Virtual software projects are assigned to groups. Typical scenarios are designed in the projects to help students understand the ten knowledge areas by solving the issues in the projects through group discussion and collaboration.

syllabus: This course introduces the fundamentals and practical implementation of machine intelligence systems. Machine intelligence refers to intelligent machines and software that rely on algorithms to reason over observed data in order to make useful predictions and decisions. The course integrates concepts from machine learning, artificial intelligence, data modelling, and computation. Core topics include basic concepts of machine learning, supervised and unsupervised learning, basic concepts of deep learning, and the foundational principles of large language models (LLMs). Students study modern deep learning architectures, including neural networks and Transformer-based models, as well as current frontier research topics such as efficient inference for large-scale models. The course places strong emphasis on hands-on practice. Practical components include Python-based machine learning using scikit-learn, deep learning implementation using TensorFlow 2 / Keras, data processing, data analysis, and model training. Students also complete practical exercises and a course project involving the deployment or application of trained machine learning models. The course is designed to be challenging and research-oriented, exposing students to both theoretical foundations and applied techniques in modern machine learning and artificial intelligence systems.
textbooks: Aurelien Geron, Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow, 2nd Edition, O?Reilly Media, 2019. The course draws from chapters covering machine learning fundamentals, supervised and unsupervised learning methods, model training and evaluation, neural networks, deep learning with TensorFlow/Keras, and practical machine learning workflows. Additional lecture materials are provided by the teaching team to cover large language models, Transformer architectures, and recent advances in machine intelligence research.

Machine intelligence refers to intelligent machines and software that rely on algorithms to reason over observed data in order to make useful predictions and decisions. The course integrates concepts from machine learning, artificial intelligence, data modelling, and computation. Core topics include basic concepts of machine learning, supervised and unsupervised learning, basic concepts of deep learning, and the foundational principles of large language models (LLMs). Students study modern deep learning architectures, including neural networks and Transformer-based models, as well as current frontier research topics such as efficient inference for large-scale models. The course places strong emphasis on hands-on practice. Practical components include Python-based machine learning using scikit-learn, deep learning implementation using TensorFlow 2 / Keras, data processing, data analysis, and model training. Students also complete practical exercises and a course project involving the deployment or application of trained machine learning models. The course is designed to be challenging and research-oriented, exposing students to both theoretical foundations and applied techniques in modern machine learning and artificial intelligence systems.
textbooks: Aurelien Geron, Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow, 2nd Edition, O?Reilly Media, 2019. The course draws from chapters covering machine learning fundamentals, supervised and unsupervised learning methods, model training and evaluation, neural networks, deep learning with TensorFlow/Keras, and practical machine learning workflows. Additional lecture materials are provided by the teaching team to cover large language models, Transformer architectures, and recent advances in machine intelligence research.

comments: The aim of the course is to 1) to enhance the previous knowledge of database systems by deepening the understanding of the theoretical and practical aspects of the database technologies; showing the need for distributed database technology to tackle deficiencies of centralized database systems; 2) to introduce basic principles and implementation techniques of distributed database systems, including distributed database design and architecture, query processing and optimization, transaction management, recovery, and reliability protocols; 3) to expose active and emerging research issues in distributed database systems and application development, including parallel and streaming data management, data warehousing and OLAP, NoSQL and NewSQL; 4) to apply theory to practice by building a data center in a distributed context.
syllabus: The course content consists of two parts: (1) Theoretical study of distributed database systems. It covers the core of principles of distributed database management systems, including database design, architecture of Distributed Database Management System (DDBMS), concurrency control, distributed transaction management, and failure recovery, and some latest development including parallel and streaming data management, data warehousing and OLAP, NoSQL, and NewSQL. (2) Experimental DDBMS. Students are organized in teams to design and implement a data center in a distributed context

syllabus: This course introduces modern computer architecture, which focuses on the hardware/software interface and the internal structural organization of computer systems. It covers the major hardware components and key design techniques in computer architecture, including systemperformance and efficiency metrics, instructions and instruction set architectures, processor structures, memory hierarchies, IO devices, and hardware specialization techniques. From an architectural perspective, the course focuses on the high-level functionalities and interaction of the system components, and abstracts away the low-level implementation details. It demonstrates how to optimize the performance and efficiency of the software through better understanding the architecture of the hardware. In addition, the course introduces the support for parallelism and specialization in modern computer systems as advanced topics, considering the ubiquity of parallel computing and specialized computing nowadays. The course also briefly introduces several state- of-the-art research advances. The lab assignments involve the assembly- level code analysis and optimization, the processor pipeline simulation, the cache functional implementation, and more. Upon the completion of the course, students will understand the basic concepts and the main functionalities of the system components, as well as howthey interact with each other. They will also learn the analysis methodology and the design principles for computer architecture, and be introduced to the tradeoffs between performance, efficiency, and cost in computer systems

syllabus: This course aims to cultivate students' skills in unmanned system development represented by UAVs. Through a combination of theory and practical case teaching, students will understand the control, communication, positioning, and other solutions of UAV platforms, as well as practice programming. Students will complete specific tasks using UAV platforms. This course involves fundamental ROS knowledge, Python programming, simulation environment development, and real UAV development. The first part of the course mainly introduces the basics of ROS, including ROS framework, basic commands, ROS communication mechanisms, and ROS messages. Students will learn how to configure the ROS development environment, understand ROS topics, services, and parameters, and how to use ROS messages and ROS parameters. The second part introduces Python programming and UAV flight control. Students will learn Python basics, functions, classes, exception handling, and build UAV control logic based on Python. The focus is on using Python to realize UAV flight control, laying a foundation for subsequent control algorithm development and simulation environment construction. The third part introduces simulation environment development. Students will learn how to use Gazebo for environment construction, UAV import, UAV navigation, and UAV attitude control. They will also learn how to use RViz for data visualization, displaying UAV status and motion trajectory. The fourth part introduces real UAV development. Students will complete UAV autonomous flight tasks, conduct real environment tests, and optimize UAV control algorithms. The final stage is a comprehensive experimental project. Students will complete a comprehensive project, design, and implement a UAV demonstration system based on specific tasks provided. syllabus: This course covers core network security technologies, including firewalls, intrusion detection systems (IDS), antivirus solutions, encryption, authentication, and Virtual Private Network (VPN) technologies. The course integrates theoretical instruction with real- world security solutions to ensure that students can apply what they learn. For the more abstract topics?such as encryption, authentication, and VPNs?the course emphasizes the importance of connecting individual concepts to form a coherent understanding. Students will gain insight into the practical integration of cryptographic algorithms, certificate authority (CA) systems, and how encryption and authentication are used in VPNs. Firewall technology, a mature and widely used security measure, is explored in depth with a focus on core terminology and practical deployment in real-world networks. Intrusion detection is introduced as a critical complement to firewalls, and antivirus technologies are discussed as indicators of the overall maturity of firewall-based systems. The course also includes a concise introduction to common attack techniques, helping students shift perspective from solely defense to understanding offensive methods. Experiencing the role of a basic attacker can spark greater interest and insight into defensive technologies. The course content is structured around currently popular and widely applied network security methods, all of which relate closely to students' everyday internet usage. This approach aims to build interest while laying a strong foundation for further exploration of network security. The course emphasizes a balance of theory and practice, reinforcing conceptual knowledge through small lab assignments and hands-on experiments. By the end of the course, students are expected to understand the key concepts and principles of network security, be familiar with various security technologies used in computing and network systems, and develop basic practical and operational skills necessary for future research or work in the field of network security.

Through a combination of general theories and specific case studies, students will learn and master solutions to key challenges in drone operation such as control, communication, and positioning. The first part of the course introduces basic ROS concepts, including the ROS framework, basic ROS commands, communication mechanisms, and message handling. The second part focuses on Python programming and drone flight control. Students will learn Python syntax, functions, classes, and exception handling, followed by drone modeling techniques. The main objective is to use Python to implement drone flight control, laying the groundwork for control algorithm development and simulation setup. The third part covers simulation environment development. Students will learn to use Gazebo for drone simulation, including scene creation, drone integration and loading, and sensor configuration. They will also learn to use Rviz for simulation visualization, showing drone status and flight trajectories. The fourth part focuses on real-world drone development. Students will complete autonomous flight tasks and test and optimize control algorithms in real-world scenarios. The final segment of the course is an integrated project. Students will design and implement a drone demonstration system based on a specific task provided by the instructors.
